passages.happening:
Moses and the elders give an order for the day Israel crosses the Jordan. The people are to set up large stones on Mount Ebal and coat them with plaster. “Write on them all the words of this law when you have crossed over to enter the land” (verse 3). The writing is to be plain to read (verse 8).

They are also to build an altar there, of whole stones that no iron tool has touched (verses 5-6). On it they will offer burnt offerings and peace offerings, ‘eating them and rejoicing in the presence of the LORD your God’ (verse 7).

Then Moses and the priests speak to the whole people. “Be silent, O Israel, and listen! This day you have become the people of the LORD your God. You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
The laws are finished. Chapters 27 and 28 now seal the covenant, as the treaties of that world were sealed, with a ceremony and with blessings and curses.

The ceremony is to be held in the middle of the land, not at its edge. Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim stand on either side of a narrow valley in the central hills, with the old town of Shechem between them. Shechem was where God first promised the land to Abraham. Israel's first act in the land is to go to the place of the first promise and set up God's law there.

Writing on plastered stone was a known practice. Stones were coated with lime plaster, and the text was written on the smooth surface. Kings of the ancient world set up great inscribed monuments to announce their victories and their laws. Israel's monument announces no king's deeds. It carries God's teaching, standing in the open where anyone can read it. Verse 8 asks for it to be written ‘distinctly’. The law is public. It is not the secret of priests or rulers.

The altar of uncut stones follows a rule given at Sinai. The reason may be to keep Israel's altars unlike the carved altars of other peoples, or to keep human skill from taking credit in worship.

Notice what stands on the mountain: the law, written out, and beside it an altar for sacrifice and a meal eaten with joy. The law and the provision for failure stand together.

Then ‘this day’. Moses has said ‘today’ all through the book. Here he says it of Israel's very identity. They became God's people at Sinai, forty years before. He says they have become his people today. Every time the covenant is heard and accepted, it is as though for the first time. And notice the order of verses 9 and 10. First, you are God's people. Therefore, obey. Belonging comes before the command.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua records that it was done: “At that time Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal to the LORD, the God of Israel”, and ‘Joshua inscribed on the stones a copy of the law of Moses’ (Joshua 8:30, 32).

The rule for the altar was given at Sinai: “Now if you make an altar of stones for Me, you must not build it with stones shaped by tools” (Exodus 20:25).

The prophet Jeremiah looked for the day when the law would be written somewhere better than stone: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).
passages.asks: Israel was to write God's law where everyone could read it and then eat with joy beside it. Ask whether God's word is something you hold in the open or keep out of sight. And hear the order of verses 9 and 10. Ask whether you obey in order to belong, or because you already do.

passages.happening:
Moses arranges the tribes. Six are to stand on Mount Gerizim for the blessing, and six on Mount Ebal for the curse (verses 12-13).

Then the Levites are to call out twelve sentences in a loud voice, and after each one all the people are to say, ‘Amen’.

The twelve are these. Cursed is the one who makes an idol ‘and sets it up in secret’ (verse 15). Cursed is the one who dishonors father or mother (verse 16), who moves a neighbor's boundary stone (verse 17), who ‘lets a blind man wander in the road’ (verse 18), who ‘withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow’ (verse 19). Four curses name sexual acts within the family or with an animal (verses 20-23). Cursed is the one who strikes a neighbor down ‘in secret’ (verse 24), and the one who takes a bribe to kill an innocent person (verse 25).

The last gathers up the rest. ‘Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice.’ And the people say, ‘Amen’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
A curse in the Bible is a solemn declaration that a person stands under God's judgment and outside his favor. The word ‘cursed’ comes twelve times, perhaps once for each tribe. Heard aloud, the repetition is heavy.

The key to the list is in the first curse and the eleventh. Both say ‘in secret’. Nearly everything on the list is something done where no one can see: an idol hidden in the house, a boundary stone shifted at night, a blind man sent the wrong way, a bribe taken, a wrong inside the family that no one outside will ever hear of. These are the sins no court can reach, because there are no witnesses.

So the people place themselves under God's own judgment. Where the judge at the gate cannot see, God can.

‘Amen’ comes from a Hebrew root meaning firm or sure. To say it was to accept the terms. Each person in the valley called the curse down on himself if he should do the thing named. No one could later say that he had not agreed.

Look at who is protected by the list. It protects parents in old age, the neighbor whose land can be stolen, the blind, the foreigner, the orphan and the widow, the members of a household who can be abused in private, and the innocent person whose death can be bought. The curses stand guard over people who cannot guard themselves.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

The last curse reaches everyone. It names no single act. It names every failure to do what the law says. No one who said that last ‘Amen’ honestly could think himself safe.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua says that when the ceremony was held, both parts were read: “Afterward, Joshua read aloud all the words of the law”, the blessings and the curses (Joshua 8:34).

Leviticus has the law behind the curse of verse 18: “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 19:14).

Paul quotes the last curse to show that the law cannot be the way anyone is put right with God. “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law’” (Galatians 3:10). He then says where the curse went: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

Paul also says that the secret things this chapter names will be judged: there is a day ‘when God will judge men’s secrets through Christ Jesus’ (Romans 2:16).
passages.hard:
Six tribes stand on Gerizim to bless. Why does the chapter give only curses?

Readers have long noticed it. Verses 12 and 13 set out a ceremony with two sides, and verses 15 to 26 record only one.

Some think the blessings are supplied by the first fourteen verses of chapter 28, which follow at once, and that this chapter records only the part the Levites spoke. Others think the twelve curses were a separate act, a kind of public self-examination, distinct from the ceremony of blessing and curse between the mountains. The book of Joshua says that Joshua read both.

The weight on the curses fits the chapter's purpose. These are sins that no human court could punish, so the people put themselves directly under God's judgment. It also prepares for the sober tone of the next three chapters, which look ahead to Israel's failure and exile.

The chapter does not deny the blessing. It makes clear that the covenant is in earnest.

These curses are part of a covenant ceremony in ancient Israel. They are not words for anyone to speak over another person today, and no one may use them to tell a suffering person that God has cursed them.
passages.asks: Almost every sin on this list is one that could be hidden for a lifetime. Ask what you do, or have done, that depends on no one finding out. And ask who is protected by your honesty in private: an aging parent, a person who trusts your directions, or someone in your own house. The chapter says that God sees what the court cannot.
